processing: A cultivar rather than a finished tea. Its trial samples were made as baked green tea (hong qing): fixed, rolled and dried with hot air, the usual route for Yunnan large-leaf greens.
harvest_season: No picking calendar specific to this cultivar is documented; as with other Yunnan large-leaf greens, spring is the prized picking.
appearance_dry: Typical of baked greens from large-leaf Yunnan bushes: sturdy dark green strips with visible down, since the young shoots are quite hairy.
appearance_liquor: As is usual for Yunnan baked greens, a bright yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Large, yellow-green shoots, as the cultivar's leaf type would suggest.
taste_profile: No tasting notes specific to this cultivar are published in plain language; expect what is typical of Yunnan large-leaf greens, a fuller, more bitter-edged cup than most eastern Chinese greens.

brewing.notes: General advice for Yunnan large-leaf greens: keep the water cooler than you would for an oolong, because this leaf turns bitter quickly.

vintage_note: You are unlikely to see this name on a retail packet; a cultivar reaches the market inside teas sold under a place or factory name. Green tea from it would be sold as usual for its class, the current year's spring picking, and is best drunk within a year.
description:
Yunkang 47 is a tea plant, not a tea you order by name. It is a cultivar bred in Yunnan at the tea research institute of the provincial academy of agricultural sciences, selected from the Nannuo large-leaf population.

The plant is a tree-type bush with large leaves, an open habit and yellow-green shoots carrying a fair amount of down. Breeders describe it as high-yielding, hardy and good in quality, and they judged it mainly as a green tea cultivar.

Little has been written about how it tastes in the cup. Assume the general character of Yunnan large-leaf greens: more body and bitterness than a Zhejiang green, so cooler water and shorter steeps help.

If you want to meet it, ask a Yunnan green tea seller which cultivar their garden uses. A packet naming it outright is rare, and any lot sold under this name deserves a question about the garden behind it.
history:
Yunkang 47 was bred by selection from Nannuo large-leaf tea, using the national-level cultivar Yunkang 10 as the control in regional trials. A 2013 paper by Xu Pizhong and colleagues in the Southwest China Journal of Agricultural Sciences set out those results and recommended it for Yunnan and tea regions with a similar climate.

Little is documented about how widely it has been planted since.
sources_note: Details come from a search snippet of the 2013 paper; the snippet did not tie the text to one specific URL, so no URL is cited.
